Pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong was first imprisoned in 2020 [File: AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP, AP and ReutersPublished On 5 Nov 20265 Nov 2026
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, who has been in prison since 2020, has been jailed for an additional 10 years.
Hong Kong’s High Court found Wong guilty of colluding with foreign entities in violation of the city’s national security law on Thursday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Jimmy Lai sentenced: What happened to other HK pro-democracy protesters?list 2 of 3Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in national security caselist 3 of 3What we know about jailed HK activist Joshua Wong’s latest chargeend of list
The sentence comes just two months before he was expected to be released in January 2027.
“The punishment must fit the gravity of ⁠the crime,” High Court Judge William Tam told a packed courtroom while delivering the sentence.
“It is also necessary for the court to express the community’s abhorrence of the defendant’s scheme and acts with others to collude with foreign forces or external elements to endanger national security.”
Wong, now 30, was accused of conspiring with self-exiled activist Nathan Law and others to ask foreign countries, bodies or individuals outside China to impose sanctions or blockades, or engage in other hostile activities against the government.
He pleaded guilty to the charge in September. Tam said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it to 10 because of Wong’s guilty plea and mitigation.
Wong was once the face of Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement and has been in jail since 2020. He was imprisoned over his role in protests held a year earlier.

South Korea plans to expand its anti-piracy patrols off the coast of Somalia to waters closer to the Strait of Hormuz, the Ministry of National Defense said, following pressure from the United States to provide support for the war on Iran.
The government will ask the National Assembly to extend the mandate of the Cheonghae unit, a naval task force due to expire at the end of 2026, a Defence Ministry spokesperson told the Reuters news agency on Thursday. The request would also widen the unit’s area of operations to waters near the port of Duqm in Oman, about 650km (403 miles) from the Strait of Hormuz.

(Al Jazeera)By Marium AliPublished On 5 Nov 20265 Nov 2026
Ten years ago, the Paris Agreement entered into force, binding nearly every country to a shared goal: to hold global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5C (2.7F).
A decade on, the deal has helped drive stronger climate policies and a rapid expansion of clean energy. But emissions remain near record highs, temperatures keep climbing and countries are still far from the cuts needed to keep a 1.5C limit within reach.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at what the Paris Agreement set out to do, how far global temperatures have risen since and which countries are driving emissions.
What is the Paris Agreement?
The Paris Agreement is a legally binding climate treaty adopted by 196 parties at the United Nations climate summit in Paris, also known as COP21, on December 12, 2015. It entered into force on November 4, 2016.
The United States, the world’s second-largest greenhouse gas emitter after China, has joined and left the agreement twice. President Donald Trump ordered both withdrawals. The first took effect in November 2020, and President Joe Biden rejoined in February 2021. The US left again in January this year, 12 months after Trump ordered its exit for a second time.
Today, 194 parties, 193 countries and the European Union, belong to the agreement.(Al Jazeera)
Rather than imposing the same cuts on everyone, the agreement asks each government to set its own targets through nationally determined contributions, or NDCs, outlining how it will cut emissions and adapt to climate change. Advertisement

New Zealand's Prime Minister and National Party leader Christopher Luxon campaigns in his Botany electorate, Auckland, New Zealand, October 26, 2026 [David Rowland/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 5 Nov 20265 Nov 2026
Days ahead of New Zealand’s election, polls show the governing centre-right National Party and the opposition centre-left Labour Party neck and neck, with neither on course to win enough seats to govern alone.
The outcome of the November 7 election could be decided by smaller parties under the country’s unique electoral system.
Recommended Stories list of 2 itemslist 1 of 2New Zealand PM Christopher Luxon calls national election for November 7list 2 of 2New Zealand deputy PM heckled day after saying colonisation good for Maoriend of list
Here is what you need to know:
How does the election work?
New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional (MMP) system.
Voters cast two ballots: one for a candidate in their local electorate and one for a party.
Winning candidates in each of the country’s 71 electorates take their seats automatically. There are seven electorates reserved for Maori, New Zealand’s Indigenous people. Maori voters can choose to enrol on either the Maori electoral roll or the general roll.
The party vote decides how many seats each party gets overall. About 49 more seats are filled from party lists so that each party’s share of parliament matches its proportional share of the vote.
A party needs either 5 percent of the party vote, or one electorate win, to get a seat. In New Zealand’s 120-seat parliament, a majority usually means 61.
